items.title: Forty Sites
items.stakes: Maya's first week as estate systems lead: a conformance number, a contractor with a template, and a boardroom that echoes.

items.rumor: Forty sites. Forty ways of doing it. Some of them on purpose.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #62 · AVERY'S LENS  Measure drift, not difference  A number that counts every difference as a failure pushes people to erase good design. Measure what nobody decided.  The conformance dashboard counted Valmera's required hearing loop as a failure. A contractor ‘fixed’ it, and every call to HQ began to echo.

Since the conformance contractor visited last month.

items.title: Conformance isn't correctness.
items.body: The template set the echo canceller's reference to output 1. In Valmera, output 1 feeds the hearing loop that the regional accessibility code requires — and the loop carries the presenter as well as HQ. The loudspeakers are on output 2. A canceller can only remove what it's told the loudspeakers play; told the wrong thing, it lets HQ's voice come straight back.
items.label: Test: why does HQ hear itself — and what pushed the change?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Adaeze beside a board. Henrik's sixty-two percent counts every difference as a failure. What should that number actually tell him? Whether rooms work as designed — so a recorded regional design counts. Three-seventy-two plus ninety-six, over six hundred… seventy-eight. And the twenty-two percent left is drift. That's the number worth shrinking.

items.title: Broad gauge and the Gauge Act
items.body: Britain's early railways were built to different track widths. In 1846 Parliament required new passenger lines to use the ‘standard’ 4 ft 8½ in gauge — but let the Great Western Railway keep its 7 ft broad gauge, which its engineer had chosen for speed and stability. The two ran side by side for decades, with mixed-gauge track and change-of-train stations, until the Great Western converted its last broad-gauge line in 1892. A standard, a recorded exception, and the long cost of both.

items.title: Sixty-two percent of what?
items.body: Adaeze and Maya sample every flagged room against its site file. Of 228, 96 are recorded regional designs — 230 V kit, 50 fps cameras, loops, bilingual panels — each with a reason and an owner. 132 have no record at all. The scan was counting differences. Only 132 of them are drift.
items.label: Test: how much of the estate is drift — and what should December's target measure?

items.alt: A bar across 600 rooms: 372 green (match the template), 96 teal (recorded regional designs), 132 red (drift, no record). Below: working as designed 78%, drift 22%.
items.caption: Seventy-eight percent working as designed. Twenty-two percent nobody decided.

items.title: any difference = FAIL
items.body: The conformance script, line 14: if value ≠ template: result = FAIL. No lookup of the site file, the exception register or the regional variants. It can't tell a hearing loop from a taped-on USB hub.

items.body: Valmera's site design file, page 3: ‘Boardroom induction loop on output 1 — required by the regional accessibility code §9 (invented); approved L. Ferreira-Amaro.’ It had been there for four years. Nobody at HQ had opened it.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Difference isn’t drift. Before you “fix” a non-conforming room, open its site file: a recorded, owned, approved difference is design; a difference with no reason, no owner and no end date is drift. Measure drift (% of rooms), not difference — and let the tools read the register. An echo canceller’s reference must be exactly what the loudspeakers play.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Think of a rule you follow at work. Which of the exceptions to it are written down — and which just happened?
